prompt: Which property means 'the same input always produces the exact same sequence of intermediate steps'?
explanation: Determinismus concerns the steps taken; Determiniertheit only concerns the final output being identical for identical input.

prompt: Name the three components of a standard correctness proof for an in-place sorting algorithm.
explanation: Termination (the loop/recursion ends), sortedness (output satisfies the ordering, usually via loop invariant), and the permutation property (no elements lost or invented).

prompt: Which of these is a legitimate reason to deliberately use a LESS efficient algorithm?
options: A constant-time algorithm avoids leaking secret information through timing (a side-channel), even though a faster-on-average algorithm exists
It's never legitimate -- the most efficient algorithm is always the correct choice
Less efficient algorithms are always easier to implement in any language
Compilers automatically upgrade inefficient code to efficient code, so it doesn't matter
explanation: Runtime itself can leak information (e.g. a password check that returns faster on an early mismatch reveals how many characters matched) -- a deliberately constant-time algorithm avoids this even at an average-case efficiency cost.

prompt: In a loop invariant that tracks 'the largest index where a chain of conditions has held so far', what boolean variable is typically needed alongside the index itself, and why?
acceptedAnswers: a flag that latches false once the condition fails
a boolean that stays false forever once it becomes false
explanation: Once the run-condition fails at some index, it must never be considered valid again for any later index, even if that later index would locally satisfy the condition -- a flag that only ever flips true-to-false (never back) enforces this.
